commenti.body:
Recently watched *An American in Paris* (1951).

Do you agree with the general perception of it as a weaker Best Picture winner? 

James Beradinelli: "The Academy loved *An American in Paris* \- an overreaction to a popular, frothy motion picture. It's a fine, fun film with a lot of great songs and dancing but there's nothing about this production that causes it to stand out when compared to one of dozens of musicals from the era." 

Erik Beck: "it didn’t belong in the race, let alone to steal Best Picture away from *Streetcar* (or, more likely, *Place*).  It’s a good enough film.  It’s enjoyable.  But it’s not great."

I watched Laura, which is leaving the criterion channel this month. I'm a gay person, but the gay subplot makes me scratch my head, unless the audience is supposed to see us as pathetic and sick people, like the killer. The maid is obviously head over heels for Laura and in one scene a handsome young man gets close enough to kiss Waldo; he responds by threatening to crack his head open if he gets any closer. Maybe the unwanted advance was to give him a taste of his own medicine and hint at his violent nature.

I loved it. Streetcar pissed me off when they cut out that Allen was gay. By changing it to him being weak, the plot made no sense. It destroys the picture. Blanche walk in on him receiving anal from the doctor. That’s why he shoots himself in the head. Streetcar the film is a classic but they ruin the plot because of the censors. Being weak and backsliding is no reason to off yourself. Getting caught receiving anal from an old friend however… American in Paris is a beautiful film with great dancing. I’d rather have it than a film that ruins itself buy complying with censors.

Rewatch of Broadcast News (1987). This is one of my favourite films from the 80s, but haven't seen it for many years. It's still an excellent, brilliantly written, engaging and entertaining film. What strikes me now is how slow the pace of many scenes is. The actors take so many pauses in between lines. The storyline with the date rape news feature is interesting to watch now - things have changed so much since the 80s. The highlight of the film is still the 'Tom is the devil' scene. Dialogue this good...   it's boring to say because it's said so often, but dialogue of this quality really doesn't find tis way into mainstream cinema any more. I wish I knew why, because there must still be great writers out there. High hopes for American Fiction - just going from the trailer it looks like potentially a throwback to solid middle-brow comedy/drama.

I became interested in the silent film era. I am aware about some classics like Metropolis, Nosferatu, Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton films. This sub seems to be the right place to ask for some recommendations regarding must watch films of this time period.

*Häxan*

*A Story of Floating Weeds*

*The Wind*

*The Last Laugh*

*Grass*

*The Adventures of Prince Achmed*

Harold Lloyd movies

My personal favorite is *Les Vampires*, a serial that can be either watched as is over a full day or over several days as a mini-series. Fun, aesthetically influential and surprisingly modern, while also providing a great basis for Oliver Assayas' *Irma Vep*, an excellent film about the production of a contemporary remake of the film. For other French silents I'd highly recommend Abel Gance's work, especially his Napoleon remains monumental even today.

Another favorite is the early Ozu, *I Was Born But...*. Partly due to the reliance and popularity of the benshi, the segue into sound films came much later in Japan than in the west, and Ozu made several fine silents during the 30s. Another user mentioned *A Story of Floating Weeds* which is also worth recommending. The Japanese silents are quite interesting as much of early non-western cinema developed in a slightly different way before the hegemony of Hollywood. Ozu, in particular, has been studied much in this context.
